AboutPage.metaDescription: Full-stack engineer with 5+ years building distributed systems, AI tools, and scalable products. Based in Germany.

AboutPage.bio4: My current focus is on the intersection of distributed systems and AI — building things that are fast, reliable, and actually solve business problems. I write occasionally on %%LINKS%% — the last article got 5K+ views.

faqHr.a: Based in Chemnitz, Germany. Open to roles across Germany, the EU, UK, US, UAE, Canada, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, and Australia — remote-first works too.
One month, at my current role with Infineon Technologies.

faqHr.q: Are you open to contract or freelance work?
faqHr.a: Open to full-time contract roles. For freelance work, only through an intermediary/EOR platform like remozo.com.

faqHr.q: What are your long-term career goals?
faqHr.a: I'm working toward German citizenship, so I'm looking for a stable role I can grow in over the next 5 years — ideally at the intersection of distributed systems and AI.
Building Infineon's Parking Guidance System from the ground up — backend, frontend, and the embedded computer vision — replacing a paid vendor and now serving 8,000 users.

faqHr.q: What motivates you to perform well at work?
faqHr.a: Building things that create measurable impact, plus a genuine love of technology — it's what got me into engineering in the first place.

faqHr.q: How do you stay current with industry trends?
faqHr.a: Hands-on experimentation — I hold Anthropic certifications in the Claude API/SDK and Claude Code, and I write the occasional article (the last one hit 5K+ views across Habr, Dev, and Medium).

faqHr.q: Can you give an example of working as part of a team to achieve a goal?
faqHr.a: Leading a 3-person team on the NCahoots admin app at WeDo.agency — I introduced React and set up linting, formatting, and pre-commit hooks to keep quality consistent across the team.

faqHr.q: What do you consider the most important qualities for success?
faqHr.a: Speed — shipping fast and iterating matters more today than getting the design perfect upfront.
Currently targeting €50–70K/year, which also covers the EU Blue Card salary threshold.

faqTech.q: How do you approach code quality and mentoring?
faqTech.a: I set up automated quality gates early — linters, formatters, pre-commit hooks — so code review can focus on design instead of style, and I've mentored several developers along the way.

faqTech.q: Do you have production on-call experience?
faqTech.a: Yes — I've built and operated services handling real traffic at Infineon and OZON Tech, including Kubernetes deployments monitored with Prometheus and Grafana.

faqTech.q: How do you approach architecture decisions?
faqTech.a: Trade-off driven, documented as ADRs — see the Decisions page for real examples from past projects.

faqTech.q: Can I see your code or side projects?
faqTech.a: Check the Skills page for an interactive breakdown of my stack, or Projects for full case studies.

faqTech.q: How do you decide when to refactor vs. rewrite?
faqTech.a: I default to refactor — most systems don't need a rewrite, just the parts that changed most often cleaned up first. A rewrite only makes sense when the architecture itself is the blocker.

faqTech.q: How do you approach system design for scalability?
faqTech.a: Start from real load, not a hypothetical one — at OZON Tech I designed a Go microservice that searches 200M warehouse items in under 5 seconds using ElasticSearch and Kafka, load-tested before it ever shipped.

faqTech.q: What's your approach to incident response?
faqTech.a: Fix first, understand second, prevent third. I've run production on-call at Infineon and OZON Tech with Kubernetes deployments monitored through Prometheus and Grafana, so the goal is catching a regression on a dashboard before a customer does.

faqTech.q: How do you evaluate whether to adopt a new technology?
faqTech.a: I prototype it against a real problem I already have, not a toy example — that's how RAG, LangChain, and MCP earned a place in my stack, and how plenty of other tools didn't.

faqTech.q: How do you handle disagreements about technical direction?
faqTech.a: Write the trade-offs down as an ADR and let the data settle it where possible — most 'disagreements' turn out to be unstated assumptions about priorities.

Tests should catch the failure modes that actually happen in production, not just hit a coverage number — unit tests plus load tests were what let me ship the OZON search service with confidence at 200M-item scale.

faqTech.q: How do you use AI in your development workflow?
faqTech.a: Claude Code paired with TDD — tests are what make AI-generated code trustworthy, not just fast. I'm also familiar with structured agentic workflows like GSD and Superpowers for keeping AI-assisted development disciplined.

faqBusiness.q: Can you work directly with a non-technical founder?
faqBusiness.a: Yes — at WeDo.agency I shipped 9 startup projects working directly with founders, translating business goals into technical scope.

faqBusiness.q: How do you scope an MVP?
faqBusiness.a: I focus on the smallest slice that proves the business hypothesis, then iterate — happy to walk through trade-offs openly.

faqBusiness.q: Are you open to fractional or part-time engagements?
faqBusiness.a: Yes — open to discussing scope, time commitment, and rates directly.

faqBusiness.q: What kind of ROI have you delivered?
faqBusiness.a: €480K/year in savings at Infineon, €86K at OZON Tech, and an 11.63% metric uplift at onlineTours — see the Impact Dashboard for details.

faqBusiness.q: Have you built something from 0 to 1 before?
faqBusiness.a: Yes — I built Infineon's Parking Guidance System from the ground up: backend, frontend, and the embedded computer vision, taking it from an idea to a live system used by 8,000 people.

faqBusiness.q: How comfortable are you wearing multiple hats?
faqBusiness.a: Very — at WeDo.agency I shipped 9 different startup products, often solo, covering backend, frontend, infrastructure, and sometimes the AI/ML pieces too.

faqBusiness.q: How do you operate with ambiguous or incomplete requirements?
faqBusiness.a: I ship the smallest version that tests the real assumption, then let actual usage tell me what to build next — that's how I scope every MVP.

faqBusiness.q: Are you open to equity as part of compensation?
faqBusiness.a: Open to discussing it as part of the overall package, especially for a role with real ownership — happy to talk specifics directly.

faqBusiness.q: What's your risk tolerance for joining an early-stage company?
faqBusiness.a: I've spent a year at WeDo.agency shipping fast for early-stage clients, so I'm comfortable with the pace — that said, I'm currently looking for a role I can commit to long-term.

faqBusiness.q: How do you move fast without breaking things?
faqBusiness.a: Automate the guardrails instead of skipping them — I've gotten CI/CD pipelines down to under 10 seconds per deploy, which means shipping quickly without losing the safety net.

ipoSim.title: How a Cyprus IPO actually pays out
ipoSim.description: Taking speechki.com public meant more than good numbers — it meant walking this exact sequence, where only one party's payday is fixed and everyone else is betting on where the market lands.
ipoSim.hint: Drag the slider below to set the sale price.
ipoSim.step1: Show at least $50K in real, audited profit
ipoSim.step2: Spin the IP into a fresh holding entity, clean of the old investor cap table
ipoSim.step3: An independent audit sets the company's valuation and verifies its books
ipoSim.step4: A broker buys the shares at a discount to that valuation — this is the company's actual payday
ipoSim.step5: Shares start trading freely on the exchange — the company never sees another cent from that
ipoSim.auditEstimateTemplate: An independent audit estimated the company's value at {value}
ipoSim.marketValueTemplate: The market eventually valued the company at {value}
ipoSim.companyCaption: Locked in the moment the broker buys — the market afterward doesn't change it
ipoSim.companyCaptionLeftOnTable: The payday itself was fixed — but the market re-rated the company so far above the audit that what got left on the table now outweighs it
ipoSim.brokerCaptionUp: The market re-rated the company above the audit — broker pockets the gap
ipoSim.brokerCaptionDown: The market agreed with the audit — no windfall left on the table
ipoSim.brokerCaptionLoss: The market crashed below what the broker paid — a real loss, not just a missed windfall
ipoSim.exchangeCaption: Small trading fees every period, in either direction — the company sees none of it

scalingSim.title: Why the point-update service was the real bet
scalingSim.description: The barcode scanners themselves weren't the hard part — routing them through a shared service instead of wiring each one into a single app was. Drag the slider to see why that choice matters as load grows.
scalingSim.hint: Drag the slider to change user count.
scalingSim.verticalImpossible: No single machine exists at this scale
scalingSim.nodesTemplate: {count, plural, one {# commodity node} other {# commodity nodes}}
scalingSim.ratioTemplate: At this load, horizontal scaling costs {ratio}× less than the single machine that would be needed to match it.
scalingSim.ratioImpossible: At this load, no single machine can do the job at all — only horizontal scaling works.
scalingSim.ratioNone: At this load, vertical and horizontal cost about the same — the gap only opens up as load grows.
scalingSim.strategicNote: That's the real strategic payoff of this project: the old setup wired each barcode scanner directly into one legacy app, so shipping a new interface would have meant buying new scanner hardware. Routing scans through a shared point-update service decoupled the two — new terminals and app interfaces plug into the same backend, which scales out with commodity nodes instead of needing an ever-bigger central server.

cancelGame.title: Catch the cancellation before it ships
cancelGame.description: Every box travels a 24-hour pre-shipping window. Some get flagged for cancellation mid-transit — press and hold one for a second to catch it before it hits the wall. Miss it, and it ships anyway.
cancelGame.legend: €8 shipping + €35 goods = €43 lost on every flagged box that reaches the wall — illustrative numbers, not real ones.
cancelGame.lostTemplate: {count, plural, one {# box} other {# boxes}} shipped before you caught them
cancelGame.hint: Press and hold a flagged box to catch it.
cancelGame.holdAria: Hold to cancel this order before it ships
cancelGame.strategicNote: This is the everleakproof edge case from the real project: once a lingerie order ships, it's non-returnable, so the only cancellation window is before dispatch. A human has to notice a flagged order, decide, and click in time — the support bot reacted the instant a cancellation came in, catching a window a person only sometimes makes.
